notes.definition: Metals are elements that react to form positive ions. Non-metals are elements that do not form positive ions. Most elements are metals; they are found to the left and towards the bottom of the periodic table, while non-metals are found towards the right and the top.
explanation: The periodic table can be split into metals and non-metals by a stepped (staircase) line that runs from near boron down to near astatine. Elements to the left of and below this line are metals, and the large majority of elements are metals. Elements to the right of and above the line are non-metals, such as carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur, the halogens and the noble gases. Hydrogen is a non-metal even though it is usually placed above Group 1.

The difference between metals and non-metals comes from their electronic structure. Metal atoms usually have a small number of electrons in their outer shell (one, two or three). When metals react they lose these outer electrons to gain the stable electronic structure of a noble gas, forming positive ions. For example, sodium (2,8,1) loses one electron to form Na⁺ (2,8), and magnesium (2,8,2) loses two electrons to form Mg²⁺. This is why metals are on the left of the table, where atoms have few outer electrons.

Non-metal atoms usually have four or more electrons in their outer shell, so it is easier for them to gain or share electrons than to lose them. When a non-metal reacts with a metal it gains electrons to form a negative ion, such as Cl⁻ or O²⁻. When non-metals react with each other they share electrons in covalent bonds, for example in H₂O or CO₂. Non-metals do not form positive ions. Going down a group the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and are lost more easily, which is why metals are also found towards the bottom of the table.

Metals and non-metals have different physical properties. Metals are usually shiny when freshly cut or polished, have high melting and boiling points (so most are solids at room temperature), are good conductors of electricity and heat, are malleable (can be hammered into shape) and ductile (can be drawn into wires), and often have high densities. Non-metals are usually dull, have low melting and boiling points (many are gases at room temperature), are poor conductors (insulators), are brittle when solid and have low densities.

There are exceptions, so you should use several properties together. Mercury is a metal but is a liquid at room temperature. Group 1 metals such as sodium have low densities and low melting points. Carbon is a non-metal, but graphite conducts electricity and diamond has a very high melting point. Iodine is a non-metal but its crystals are shiny.

Metals and non-metals also differ in their chemical properties. Metals react with non-metals to form ionic compounds such as sodium chloride. Metal oxides are basic: they react with acids, and those that dissolve in water form alkaline solutions (pH above 7). Non-metal oxides, such as carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide, are acidic: those that dissolve in water form acidic solutions (pH below 7). The type of ion formed (positive for metals) is the most reliable way to decide whether an element is a metal.
keyFacts: Metals are elements that react to form positive ions.
Non-metals are elements that do not form positive ions.
The majority of elements are metals.
Metals are found to the left and towards the bottom of the periodic table; non-metals to the right and towards the top.
Metal atoms usually have 1, 2 or 3 outer electrons, which they lose when they react.
Non-metal atoms usually have 4 to 7 outer electrons and gain or share electrons when they react (Group 0 atoms already have a stable arrangement).
Metals: shiny, high melting points, good conductors, malleable, ductile, often dense.
Non-metals: dull, low melting points, poor conductors, brittle when solid, low density.
Metal oxides are basic; non-metal oxides are acidic.
Exceptions: mercury is a liquid metal; graphite (carbon) is a non-metal that conducts electricity.

keyTerms.definition: An element that reacts to form positive ions.
An element that does not form positive ions; it gains or shares electrons when it reacts.
An atom or group of atoms with an electrical charge, formed by losing or gaining electrons.
Able to be hammered or pressed into shape without shattering.
Able to be drawn out into a wire.
Breaks or shatters when hit or bent.
An oxide that reacts with acids; metal oxides are basic and soluble ones form alkaline solutions.
An oxide that forms an acidic solution in water or reacts with bases; most non-metal oxides are acidic.

workedExamples.title: Classifying an element from its electronic structure
workedExamples.question: Element Q has the electronic structure 2,8,3. Is Q a metal or a non-metal? Explain your answer and give the formula of the ion it forms.
steps: Q has 3 electrons in its outer shell, so it is in Group 3.
It is easier for an atom with 3 outer electrons to lose them than to gain 5 more.
Losing 3 electrons leaves the stable structure 2,8 and a charge of 3+.
Elements that form positive ions are metals (Q is aluminium).
workedExamples.answer: Q is a metal because it loses its 3 outer electrons to form a positive ion, Q³⁺ (Al³⁺).

workedExamples.title: Using data to classify elements
workedExamples.question: Element A melts at 1085 °C, conducts electricity when solid and can be drawn into wires. Element B melts at 115 °C, is a brittle yellow solid that does not conduct, and its oxide forms a solution of pH 3. Classify A and B.
steps: A has a high melting point, conducts electricity and is ductile: these are typical metal properties.
B has a low melting point, is brittle and is an insulator: typical non-metal properties.
B's oxide is acidic (pH 3), which confirms B is a non-metal.
A is copper and B is sulfur.
workedExamples.answer: A is a metal; B is a non-metal.

workedExamples.title: Predicting the nature of an oxide
workedExamples.question: Calcium burns to form calcium oxide, CaO. Predict the pH of the solution formed when calcium oxide reacts with water, and explain your prediction.
steps: Calcium is a metal (Group 2, forms Ca²⁺ ions).
Soluble basic oxides form alkaline solutions with water (calcium hydroxide forms).
workedExamples.answer: The solution is alkaline, pH above 7 (about 12 to 13), because calcium oxide is a metal oxide and so is basic.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all metals are hard, dense solids with high melting points.
misconceptions.right: In fact mercury is a liquid at room temperature, and Group 1 metals are soft with low melting points and low densities. The reliable test is that metals form positive ions.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think no non-metal can conduct electricity.
misconceptions.right: In fact graphite, a form of the non-metal carbon, is a good conductor of electricity.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think hydrogen is a metal because it is above Group 1.
misconceptions.right: In fact hydrogen is a non-metal. It is a gas made of H₂ molecules with covalent bonds.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think non-metals form positive ions by losing their outer electrons.
misconceptions.right: In fact non-metals do not form positive ions; they gain electrons to form negative ions or share electrons in covalent bonds.

realWorld: Copper is used for electrical wiring because it is a very good conductor and is ductile.
Sulfur dioxide from burning fossil fuels is an acidic non-metal oxide that causes acid rain.
Lime (calcium oxide) is a basic metal oxide that farmers spread on fields to neutralise acidic soil.
Aluminium is used for saucepans and drinks cans because it is malleable and conducts heat well.
examTips: Learn the definition exactly: metals are elements that react to form positive ions; non-metals do not form positive ions.
When explaining with electrons, give the number of outer electrons and say whether they are lost, gained or shared, then state the ion's charge.
In data questions, use more than one property and look for exceptions; an acidic oxide or forming a negative ion is strong evidence of a non-metal.
Describe position precisely: metals to the left and towards the bottom; non-metals to the right and towards the top.
summary: Metals form positive ions; non-metals do not.
Most elements are metals, found to the left and bottom of the periodic table.
Metal atoms have few outer electrons and lose them; non-metal atoms gain or share electrons.
Metals are shiny, conductive, malleable, ductile and usually have high melting points.
Non-metals are dull, insulating, brittle and usually have low melting points.
Metal oxides are basic; non-metal oxides are acidic.

questions.question: Where are metals found in the periodic table?
options: To the left and towards the bottom
To the right and towards the top
markScheme: 1 mark: to the left and towards the bottom
questions.explanation: Metals occupy the left side and bottom; non-metals are to the right and top.

questions.question: Elements that react to form positive ions are called:
markScheme: 1 mark: metals
questions.explanation: This is the AQA definition of a metal. Non-metals, including the halogens and noble gases, do not form positive ions.

questions.question: Which property is typical of a non-metal?
markScheme: 1 mark: poor conductor of electricity
questions.explanation: Non-metals are usually insulators. Shiny, malleable and dense are metal properties.

questions.question: Most of the elements in the periodic table are:
markScheme: 1 mark: metals
questions.explanation: The majority of elements are metals. Only about 20 elements are non-metals.

questions.question: Which of these elements is a non-metal?
markScheme: 1 mark: oxygen
questions.explanation: Oxygen is in Group 6 on the right of the table. Iron, sodium and copper are all metals.

questions.question: An atom has the electronic structure 2,8,2. Which statement about this element is correct?
options: It is a non-metal because it gains 6 electrons
It is a metal because it loses 2 electrons to form a 2+ ion
It is a non-metal because it shares 2 electrons
It is a metal because it gains 2 electrons to form a 2− ion
markScheme: 1 mark: metal, loses 2 electrons, 2+ ion
questions.explanation: With 2 outer electrons (magnesium), losing 2 is far easier than gaining 6. Forming a positive ion makes it a metal.

questions.question: Element Z burns in oxygen. The oxide dissolves in water to give a solution of pH 3. Which element is Z most likely to be?
markScheme: 1 mark: sulfur
questions.explanation: An acidic solution means an acidic oxide, so Z is a non-metal. Magnesium, sodium and calcium are metals with basic oxides.

questions.question: Which non-metal has a form that conducts electricity?
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon
questions.explanation: Graphite, a form of carbon, conducts electricity. Sulfur, iodine and oxygen are insulators.

questions.question: Which ion is formed by a non-metal?
markScheme: 1 mark: Cl⁻
questions.explanation: Non-metals gain electrons to form negative ions. The positive ions are all formed by metals.

questions.question: Which metal is an exception to the rule that metals have high melting points and are solid at room temperature?
markScheme: 1 mark: mercury
questions.explanation: Mercury melts at about −39 °C so is a liquid at room temperature. Iron, copper and tungsten have high melting points.

questions.question: An element is in Group 6 and Period 3. Which description fits this element?
options: A shiny solid that conducts electricity and forms 2+ ions
A brittle yellow solid that forms 2− ions with metals
A soft metal that reacts quickly with water
markScheme: 1 mark: brittle yellow solid forming 2− ions
questions.explanation: Group 6, Period 3 is sulfur (2,8,6), a non-metal that gains 2 electrons to form S²⁻. Non-metals never form positive ions.

questions.question: Why do elements on the left of the periodic table tend to be metals?
options: Their atoms have large nuclei that attract extra electrons
Their atoms have full outer shells
Their atoms have many outer electrons that are easily shared
Their atoms have few outer electrons, which are lost more easily than extra electrons are gained
markScheme: 1 mark: few outer electrons, easily lost
questions.explanation: Atoms on the left have 1 or 2 outer electrons. Losing these gives a stable structure and forms positive ions, the defining feature of metals.

questions.question: Which observation is the best evidence that an element is a metal?
options: It has a high melting point
It forms positive ions in its compounds
It is a solid at room temperature
markScheme: 1 mark: forms positive ions
questions.explanation: Iodine is shiny, carbon has a very high melting point and many non-metals are solids, but only metals form positive ions.

questions.question: State where non-metals are found in the periodic table.
markScheme: 1 mark: to the right and towards the top
questions.explanation: Non-metals are above and to the right of the staircase line.

questions.question: Give two physical properties that are typical of metals.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: shiny / high melting or boiling point / good conductor of electricity / good conductor of heat / malleable / ductile / high density / sonorous
questions.explanation: Any two typical physical properties of metals score.

questions.question: Give two physical properties that are typical of non-metals.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: dull / low melting or boiling point / poor conductor of heat or electricity / brittle when solid / low density
questions.explanation: Non-metal properties are generally the opposite of metal properties.

questions.question: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in water. State whether the solution formed is acidic or alkaline.
markScheme: 1 mark: acidic
questions.explanation: Sulfur is a non-metal and non-metal oxides are acidic.

questions.question: Name the type of ion that metals form when they react.
markScheme: 1 mark: positive ions
questions.explanation: Metal atoms lose electrons, so the ions have more protons than electrons and are positive.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of electrons, why magnesium is a metal.
markScheme: 1 mark: magnesium atoms have 2 electrons in the outer shell
1 mark: which are lost to form a positive ion (Mg²⁺)
questions.explanation: Metals are defined by forming positive ions, which magnesium does by losing its 2 outer electrons.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of electrons, why chlorine is a non-metal.
markScheme: 1 mark: chlorine atoms have 7 outer electrons
1 mark: they gain an electron to form a negative ion (Cl⁻) or share electrons, so do not form positive ions
questions.explanation: It is easier to gain 1 electron than to lose 7, so chlorine never forms positive ions.

questions.question: Describe how the oxides of metals and non-metals differ in their chemical properties.
markScheme: 1 mark: metal oxides are basic / react with acids / form alkaline solutions (pH above 7)
1 mark: non-metal oxides are acidic / form acidic solutions (pH below 7)
questions.explanation: This acid-base difference is a key chemical property that distinguishes metals from non-metals.

questions.question:
Element X melts at 1085 °C, conducts electricity and can be drawn into wires. Element Y melts at 115 °C, is a brittle yellow solid and does not conduct electricity.
Identify which element is the metal. Give three pieces of evidence from the data.
markScheme: 1 mark: X is the metal (with at least one reason)
1 mark: high melting point and conducts electricity
1 mark: ductile / can be drawn into wires (Y is brittle, insulating, low melting point)
questions.explanation: X has three typical metal properties. Y has typical non-metal properties (it is sulfur).

questions.question: Group 4 contains carbon at the top and tin and lead at the bottom. Carbon is a non-metal but tin and lead are metals. Explain, in terms of atomic structure, why elements become more metallic going down a group.
markScheme: 1 mark: going down, atoms have more shells so outer electrons are further from the nucleus (more shielding)
1 mark: so the attraction is weaker and outer electrons are lost more easily, forming positive ions
questions.explanation: This explains why metals are found towards the bottom of the table as well as on the left.

questions.question: Silicon is a shiny grey solid with a high melting point. It is brittle and its oxide, SiO₂, is acidic. Suggest why silicon is difficult to classify as a metal or a non-metal, and use its position to suggest why.
markScheme: 1 mark: it has some properties of metals (shiny, high melting point) and some of non-metals (brittle, acidic oxide)
1 mark: it is close to the dividing (staircase) line between metals and non-metals
questions.explanation: Elements near the dividing line show a mixture of properties. Silicon's acidic oxide and the fact it does not form positive ions mean it is classed as a non-metal.

questions.question: Compare the physical and chemical properties of metals and non-metals. Explain the chemical differences in terms of the electronic structure of their atoms.
markScheme: Indicative content: metals: shiny, high melting and boiling points, good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable, ductile, high density; non-metals: dull, low melting and boiling points, poor conductors, brittle, low density; exceptions such as mercury and graphite; chemical: metals form positive ions, non-metals form negative ions or share electrons in covalent bonds; metal oxides basic, non-metal oxides acidic; metal atoms have 1 to 3 outer electrons, which are lost to give a full outer shell; non-metal atoms have 4 to 7 outer electrons and gain or share electrons to complete the outer shell.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed comparison of both physical and chemical properties, with a clear explanation linking outer electrons to ion formation.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): several correct comparisons, with some explanation in terms of electrons.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): a few simple properties listed, little or no comparison or explanation.
questions.explanation: A comparison needs both sides stated for each property. The explanation must link the number of outer electrons to losing or gaining electrons.

questions.question: Explain how the electronic structure of atoms relates to the positions of metals and non-metals in the periodic table.
markScheme: Indicative content: group number equals number of outer electrons; elements on the left (Groups 1 and 2) have 1 or 2 outer electrons, lose them easily and form positive ions, so are metals; elements on the right (Groups 5 to 7) have 5 to 7 outer electrons and gain electrons to form negative ions or share electrons, so are non-metals; Group 0 has full outer shells; going down a group outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so are lost more easily, making elements more metallic towards the bottom.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear explanation covering both left-right and top-bottom position in terms of outer electrons.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): links number of outer electrons to metal or non-metal with limited explanation.
questions.explanation: Top answers explain both directions: across a period (number of outer electrons) and down a group (distance from the nucleus).

questions.question:
A student tested four elements, A to D.
A: melting point 98 °C, conducts electricity, its oxide dissolves to form a solution of pH 13.
B: melting point −101 °C, does not conduct, forms an ion with a 1− charge.
C: very high melting point (above 3500 °C), conducts electricity, its oxide is an acidic gas.
D: melting point 1538 °C, conducts electricity, its oxide reacts with acids.
Classify each element as a metal or non-metal. Evaluate which evidence is most useful for classifying elements, referring to any elements whose properties are unusual.
markScheme: Indicative content: A is a metal (basic oxide, conducts) despite its low melting point (sodium); B is a non-metal (insulator, low melting point, forms negative ion) (chlorine); C is a non-metal (acidic oxide) despite high melting point and conductivity (carbon as graphite); D is a metal (high melting point, conducts, basic oxide) (iron); physical properties can be misleading because of exceptions (A low melting point, C conducts); chemical evidence (type of ion formed, acidic or basic oxide) is more reliable because the definition of a metal is that it forms positive ions; conclusion: use the nature of the oxide or ion, supported by several physical properties.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all four correctly classified with reasons, unusual properties identified, and a reasoned judgement that chemical evidence is most reliable.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): most classified correctly with some reasons, and some comment on reliability.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct classifications with little justification.
questions.explanation: The trap is element C: it conducts and has a high melting point but forms an acidic oxide, so it is a non-metal. Chemical properties are the reliable test.
